input.question: How much of the "snow" on an analog T.V. is from the cosmic microwave background radiation?
input.ground_truth: > but I have no idea to estimate how many pixels are actually being lit up by CMBR. Zero. And very little of the overall noise is due to CMBR Thermal noise is a much much larger contributor than CMBR (by a factor of between 100 and 1,000) to the 'snowy' picture on analog televisions. In [this](_URL_0_) thread /u/MrDerpleton provides some great information on how the 'snow' pattern becomes rendered.

Okay! Imagine your TV is like a little window that can sometimes show fuzzy stuff when there’s nothing on. That fuzzy stuff is called "snow."

Now, the "snow" you see is mostly because your TV is trying to find a signal but can’t. It’s like when you try to listen to a radio station but it’s not clear, so you just hear fuzz.

But, a *tiny* bit of that fuzziness comes from something called "cosmic microwave background radiation." This is a special kind of invisible light that comes from the very beginning of the universe, like a leftover glow from when the universe was super, super young.

But don’t worry! Most of the "snow" is just your TV being confused, not the universe talking to you. The universe’s leftover glow is way too weak for you to see on your TV. It’s like trying to see a firefly next to a big, bright light bulb. 🌌📺🔦
